unit.title: Strategies
unit.description: From buy and hold to day trading: what the evidence says about each strategy

texts: Getting out «just for a few days»
Tomás
The market's falling hard. I'll get out for a few days and come back when it calms down.
What do you tell Tomás?
Good idea: that way he dodges the worst
The best days tend to come right next to the worst ones. If he's out, he misses them.
Careful: the best days come right after the worst ones
Exactly! Of the 10 best days, 7 came very close to the worst ones.
OK, but just for one day
One day is enough: if it's one of the best, it costs a lot.
Missing just the 10 best days: **$32,871**. Less than half.
OK. I'll stay in and look at the screen less.
What if you pick the wrong country?
Real data: the Japanese stock market month by month since 1985. Invest in any month and wait a few years.
In Japan, if you invested in any month and waited **20 years**, how often did you lose money?
Never: 20 years is a very long time
About half the time
Always
**52 %** of 20-year periods ended in a loss. The Nikkei took 34 years to get back to its 1989 peak.
Stretch the wait to 30 years. Do the losses disappear?
Not even with 30 years: **36 %** of periods were still in the red. Buy and hold works better with **a broad, global index** than with a single country.
Even waiting decades doesn't make the losses go away. All from relying on one country.
With 10 years or more, close to half of the periods lost money.
Stretch the wait and see how often money was lost

steps.title: The boring strategy that works
steps.body:
Buy a broad, cheap index, **hold it for decades** and add money regularly.

According to SPIVA (end of 2025), **97 %** of European equity funds lagged their index over 10 years. Buying the index already puts you ahead of almost everyone.
steps.key: In the stock market, time in the market beats timing the market.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, open the S&P 500 ETF and look at its monthly chart.

texts: Carla's list
Carla
I've run a screen: P/E below 10 and little debt. I get **40 companies**.
I buy the ten cheapest and that's it, right?
What's missing?
Nothing: the screen has done the work
A screen only tells you what to look at. It doesn't tell you **why** they're cheap.
Reading up on each business and keeping the ones she understands
That's the **circle of competence**: you can only value well what you understand.
Buying all 40 to spread the risk
You spread the risk, but you also buy the traps. First you have to look at each business.
Of the 40, I truly understand four. And only one trades well below what I think it's worth.
Then you have **one** idea, not forty. A value investor says «no» almost every time.
Fourteen years behind
Real data, from January 2007 to December 2020: you put **€10,000** into a fund of US «value» shares (the cheap ones according to their accounts) or into a «growth» one.
US «value» shares
US «growth» shares
Over those 14 years, which style gained more?
Value, by a wide margin
About the same
Growth, with more than double
The €10,000 in value ended at **€22,849**; in growth, at **€51,293**.
Move everything to growth and compare.
Value didn't «stop working»: it gained 128 %. But whoever chose it spent **more than a decade watching the other one win**. A style only works if you can sit through its bad years.
Look at the gap. And in 2007 nobody knew which one would win.
Move the weight between value and growth

steps.title: How a value investor works
steps.body:
1. **Screen**: look for companies that are cheap according to their accounts.
2. **Understand**: keep the businesses you can explain.
3. **Value**: estimate what each one is worth and demand a margin of safety.
4. **Wait**: buy only if the price gets there, and hold for years.

Buffett calls it his **circle of competence**: it doesn't matter how big it is, but knowing where it ends.
steps.key: Value investing is more patience than formula: few purchases, well understood, and years of waiting.
steps.tip: Try it: set a price alert below what you think your favourite company is worth.

texts: A flat 8 % or a growing 3 %
Hugo
I want to live off dividends one day. I'm torn between two companies.
One pays **8 %** and hasn't raised it in years. The other pays **3 %** and raises it by **8 % every year**.
For every €1,000 invested today, which will pay him more in 15 years?
The 8 % one: it starts far ahead
It does start ahead: €80 against €30. But €30 growing 8 % every year is **€95** in year 15.
The 3 % one: by then it pays more
That's it: €30 growing 8 % a year is **€95** in year 15, against the same old €80.
Both the same
No: a fixed €80 against €30 that keeps growing. From year 13 on, the second one pays more.
Thirteen years is a long wait…
That's why it's a strategy for decades. And watch that 8 %: a very high dividend is often a warning of a cut.
More dividend, more gain?
Real data, from January 2007 to December 2025: you put **€10,000** into a fund of US **high-dividend** shares or into the whole **S&P 500**. Both with dividends reinvested.
US high-dividend shares
US shares (S&P 500)
Which one ended up with more money?
The high-dividend one: it pays out more every year
The whole S&P 500
They tied
The high-dividend fund ended at **€49,550**; the S&P 500, at **€67,475**. And in the 2008 crisis they fell almost the same: 52 % and 51 %.
Move everything to the S&P 500 and compare.
Collecting more dividends **didn't give a higher total return** over this period, nor did it protect in the fall. A dividend is a way of getting paid, not an extra gain.
What counts is the total: price plus dividends.
Move the weight between the two funds

steps.title: The toll of getting paid every year
steps.body:
In Spain, every dividend you collect is taxed **that same year** as savings income (from 19 %). An **accumulating** fund reinvests it inside and you pay nothing until you sell.

And look at **concentration**: high dividends tend to cluster in a few sectors, such as banks, utilities and telecoms. A «dividend» portfolio can end up being a bet on three sectors.
steps.key: A dividend is a way of getting paid, not an extra return: always look at total return.
steps.tip: Try it: ask Lumi which sectors pay the highest dividends in the IBEX 35.

texts: Hugo's 20 trades
Hugo
I follow trends. Of my last 20 trades, I only got 7 right.
But when I'm right I make 3 times what I risk. When I'm wrong, I lose 1.
Is Hugo making or losing money?
Losing: he's wrong almost two times out of three
7 wins of 3R make 21R; 13 losses of 1R, 13R. He's up **8R**.
Making: his wins are much bigger than his losses
Exactly! 21R won minus 13R lost: **+0.4R** per trade, before costs.
Impossible to tell
You can tell: 7 × 3R − 13 × 1R = **+8R** over 20 trades.
That's trend following: **lots of small losses and a few big wins**.
That's why I never remove my stop.
Where does it do well?
Trend following means buying what has been rising for a while and getting out when the trend breaks. Which market does it work in, and which does it struggle in?
Does well
Struggles
A rise that lasts several months
Trends of 3 to 12 months have tended to persist: this is its home turf.
A sideways market, going nowhere
It gives false signals again and again: in and out with small losses.
A sharp reversal overnight
Sharp reversals catch it still in the trade. Hence the stop.
Long trends in bonds, currencies and commodities
Studies find momentum in many markets, with data going back to 1880.
Sort the four markets.
Trends of **3 to 12 months** have tended to persist (Jegadeesh and Titman; Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen). In a **sideways** market, though, it struggles: its edge depends on cutting losses fast.
Hint: with no clear direction, there's no trend to follow.
Does well or struggles? Sort each market

steps.title: A typical rule
steps.body: Buy when the price rises above its average over many sessions, with a stop below the latest higher low, and raise the stop as it moves up.
steps.key: Momentum is one of the most studied anomalies, but it only works with discipline and risk management.
steps.tip: Try it: find an asset in an uptrend in Market and add it to Favourites.

texts: The night before earnings
Nora
I've got a buy for a few weeks, with its stop. Tomorrow the company reports earnings.
Anyway, if it goes wrong, the stop kicks in and that's that.
What would you do in her place?
Leave it as it is: the stop protects me
If it opens far lower tomorrow, the stop fills there, a long way from what you planned.
Cut the size or close before earnings
Nice! Better not to hold big positions going into earnings.
Buy more: they're bound to be good
Nobody knows how they'll turn out. Doubling up right before is gambling.
The next morning, the price opens far from the previous day's close.
That's a **gap**. In swing trading, nights and weekends count too.
How much to buy in a swing trade
A **€10,000** account. The stop goes below the recent low, **5 %** under your entry.
With 1 % risk and the stop 5 % away, what share of the account do you buy?
The whole account
A fifth
Just 1 %
You risk €100. If the stop is 5 % below, you buy **€2,000**: 20 % of the account.
Set the risk to 1 % and the stop to 5 %.
Size comes from the stop: **risk ÷ distance to the stop**. Stop, target and size are decided before you enter.
You're risking more than 1 %: a losing streak would really hurt.
With the stop further away you buy less. What you risk stays the same.
Adjust the risk and the distance to the stop

steps.title: Key takeaway
steps.body:
Swing: trades lasting **days to weeks**, on the daily chart. You aim to catch one leg: buy on a pullback or at a support within a trend and get out near resistance.

Every trade pays commission and *spread*, and the shorter the timeframe, the more false signals.
steps.key: Swing: legs lasting days or weeks, with a structural stop and a reward/risk ratio of 2:1 or more.
steps.tip: Try it: on your next simulator buy, set the stop and target before you enter.

u25l7.title: Day trading: what the data says

texts: A year of day trading
1,000 people *day trade* with no edge: every trade is a coin toss. Each one costs **€5** in commission and *spread*.
At 4 trades a day, a year comes to about 1,000. How many end up losing?
About half
Almost all of them
Hardly anyone
Costs alone: 4 × €5 × 250 days = **€5,000** a year. In the simulation, **96 %** lose.
Go all the way to a full year: 1,000 trades.

Real data looks similar: in Brazil, of those who *day traded* for more than 300 days, **97 % lost money** and only 1.1 % earned more than the minimum wage. In Taiwan, **fewer than 1 %** make money consistently after fees.
Almost all in the red. Nobody's worse than anyone else: it's the costs.
The average is already down more than €1,000. And it keeps going.
Increase each person's trades
€3,000 screenshots
@TraderDeLujo
I made **€3,000** in a day today. Here's the screenshot.
My course on making a living from trading: only €500. Last few places!
What do you do?
Buy the course: the screenshot proves it
A screenshot isn't a track record: you don't see the losses or how much they make from courses.
Ask for their full, verified track record
Nice! Chances are they don't have one. And almost everyone loses.
Ask what they're buying tomorrow
Even if they get it right once, you don't know how they do overall.
On social media you only see screenshots of wins, never the full track record.

steps.title: Why they lose
steps.body:
• **Costs:** commission and *spread* on every trade. With lots of trades a day, they eat up any small edge.
• **Competition:** professionals and algorithms with better data and near-zero costs.
• **Noise:** on minute charts, most moves mean nothing.
steps.key: The vast majority of people who day trade consistently lose money.
steps.tip: Try it: open your Portfolio history and count how many trades you made this month.

texts: The magnifying glass effect
You put up **€1,000** as margin and the broker lets you move much more. Move the leverage and the price.
At 1:10, the price drops 10 %. What happens to your €1,000?
You lose €100
You lose half
You lose the lot
You're moving €10,000: 10 % is €1,000, your entire margin. If it rises 5 %, you make 50 %; if it falls 5 %, you lose 50 %.
At 1:30, find the smallest move against you that wipes out your whole margin.
At 1:30, just **3.3 %** against you is enough to lose everything: a normal move over a couple of days. **Leverage multiplies gains and losses equally.**
Margin at zero. And the price has barely moved.
+50 %! Now move the price the other way.
Raise the leverage and move the price
Leo goes short
Leo
This share is way overpriced. I'm going short: I sell it without owning it and buy it back cheaper.
And what if, instead of falling, it rises?
What's the most Leo can lose?
What he put in, same as when buying
That's when you buy. When you're short, every euro the price rises is a loss.
In theory, there's no limit: the price has no ceiling
Exactly! The loss on a short is **unlimited**.
Nothing, because he has a stop
The stop helps, but a gap can jump right over it.
January 2021: GameStop shoots up and everyone who was short has to buy back at the same time.
OK. While I'm learning, no shorting.

steps.title: What the CNMV says
steps.body:
A **CFD** tracks an asset with leverage. Mandatory warning: «Between **74 and 89 %** of retail investor accounts lose money when trading CFDs».

In the EU (ESMA, 2018): at most **1:30** on major currency pairs, 1:20 on indices, 1:5 on shares and **1:2 on crypto**. Positions are closed if margin drops below 50 % and you can't lose more than you deposited. Keeping a position open costs daily **financing**.
steps.key: Leverage multiplies gains and losses equally, but big losses take you out of the game.
steps.tip: Try it: check in Market how much your favourite asset moves in a day.

texts: What fall could you stomach?
Real data from October 2003 to 2025, with dividends and coupons. You put in **€10,000** and choose the mix.
Tech shares (Nasdaq 100)
US shares (S&P 500)
US bonds
With everything in tech shares, how far did the portfolio fall at its worst?
Half
It never fell
It fell **50 %** in the 2008 crisis. In the end it multiplied the money more than 20 times… for anyone who didn't sell.
Find a mix whose worst fall doesn't go beyond 32 %.

With **60 %** in tech shares and the rest in bonds, the worst fall stayed at 31 % and it still gained more than 1,200 %. **The best strategy is the one you'll be able to stick with** when things go badly.
Half your money in the red. Could you hold on without selling?
A more bearable fall. Look how much it gained anyway.
Move the percentages and watch the worst fall
What suits each person?
The strategy has to fit your **time**, your **horizon**, your **temperament** and your **knowledge**.
Automatic index fund
Studying companies
Swing with a plan
Marta: 30 minutes a month and hates watching the market
Automatic contributions to an index fund: it works without her.
Pablo: loves reading company accounts
Value investing: studying businesses is exactly what he enjoys.
Ana: checks charts every day and follows rules
Swing trading with a plan and a journal: she has the time and the discipline.
Bruno: 40-year horizon and wants something simple
Buy and hold a global index, adding money every month.
Laura: works 10 hours a day and only checks her phone on breaks
She needs something that doesn't depend on watching the market.
Find each person's strategy.
There's no single best strategy for everyone: there's **the one you can stick with**. These are educational examples, not recommendations.
Hint: if they have no time, better something that works without watching.
Read each case and pick their strategy

steps.title: Core and satellite
steps.body: Lots of people separate a long-term **core portfolio** (diversified, cheap, automatic) from a **small part** for speculating or learning, with a written limit they could lose entirely.
steps.key: The boring core first; the excitement, if any, with a small, capped part.
steps.tip: Try it: in the simulator, buy a global ETF as your core and keep the satellite small.

u25l1-1.prompt: This is how the S&P 500 was doing up to October 2002. What trend do you see? (S&P 500 · weekly closes · up to the week of 07/10/2002)
u25l1-1.explanation: A 45 % fall from the 2000 high: one of those moments when the most people give up on «buy and hold».

u25l1-2.prompt: October 2002: after almost three years of falls, lots of people sell so as «not to lose any more». What did the S&P 500 do next?
u25l1-2.explanation: Those who held on (or kept investing) gradually recovered. Those who sold in the panic turned a temporary fall into a permanent loss.

u25l1-4.prompt: Match each time frame with the historical share of periods with a gain in the S&P 500.
u25l1-4.explanation: The longer the time frame, the lower the chance of losing in US history. It's not a law of physics.

u25l1-7.prompt: March 2020: the S&P 500 falls 34 % in a month because of covid. Pablo has an index fund for his retirement, 35 years away. What does he do?
options: Pauses his contributions until things calm down
Sells everything and waits for it to pass
u25l1-7.explanation: Buy and hold means sitting through the falls: that's where the strategy is won or lost.
feedback: Pausing contributions means not buying just when it's cheapest: over 35 years, that hurts him.
The index got back to its high in about 5 months. Pablo would have missed the strongest rebounds.
Good: his contributions bought cheap and within a few months the index was back at its highs.

u25l1-9.prompt: What does buy and hold need to work? Select all that apply.
u25l1-9.explanation: It needs plenty of diversification and sitting through falls without selling, as well as low costs. It doesn't need good timing, and selling at every fall is exactly the opposite: it makes you miss the rebounds.

u25l3-4.prompt: Because of a general panic, a company with stable profits, little debt and loyal customers falls 30 % in a month without its business having changed. How does a value investor see it?
options: Sells: if it's falling, something bad is going on
Checks whether the business is unchanged
Buys straight away: 30 % off has to be a bargain
u25l3-4.explanation: A value investor separates the price (which changes every day) from the value of the business (which changes slowly).
feedback: That's letting Mr Market decide for you, right on his panic day.
Good: if the value hasn't changed but the price has, there may be an opportunity. You check first.
Without analysis or diversification it isn't value investing: it's gambling.

u25l3-6.prompt: Match each concept with its meaning.
u25l3-6.explanation: These are the basic building blocks of Graham and Buffett's value investing.
right: An advantage that protects the business from competitors
The cushion between that value and the price
What you estimate the business is worth

u25l3-10.prompt: Which signs point to a possible value trap? Select all that apply.
options: A price fall caused by a general panic
Stable profits and a high ROIC
u25l3-10.explanation: Sales falling year after year and debt that keeps growing point to a trap, as does a disappearing sector. Stable profits with a high ROIC are signs of quality, and a fall caused by a general panic says nothing about the business.

u25l3-11.prompt: Lumi thinks value investing means buying whatever has fallen most: a share that went from €100 to €40 looks like a bargain to her. What do you say?
options: Yes, the more it falls, the better
Value is buying whatever is rising most
u25l3-11.explanation: Value compares price with value, not today's price with yesterday's.
feedback: Ah, OK: first I estimate the value, and only if the price is well below it is there a margin.
That's anchoring: the fact that it used to be €100 says nothing about what it's worth today.
That sounds more like momentum, which is a different strategy.
lines: Value investing means buying whatever has fallen the most, right? 📉
This share was at €100 and now it's at €40: bargain!

u25l4-7.prompt: Is it a feature of an accumulating fund or a distributing fund?
options: It pays the dividends into your account
You don't pay tax until you sell
Useful if you need a regular income
u25l4-7.explanation: While you're building wealth, accumulating funds are usually more tax-efficient.

u25l4-12.prompt: Lumi is going to buy the share with the highest dividend, 12 % a year, because it's «guaranteed income». What do you say?
options: Buy the one with the second-highest dividend too
First, check whether earnings cover it
u25l4-12.explanation: A sky-high dividend is sometimes the sign that it's about to be cut: what matters is that earnings cover it. The temptation is to look only at the size of the dividend.
feedback: Two dividends at risk don't make one safe one.
OK: if earnings are falling, that 12 % is a red flag, not a gift.
A 12 % yield usually means the price has fallen because the market expects a cut.
lines: I'm going to buy the share with the highest dividend in the Market.

u25l5-1.prompt: What trend do you see in this real chart? (Siemens · closes every 3 sessions · April–June 2026)
u25l5-1.explanation: Higher and higher highs and lows: this is trend-follower territory.

u25l5-2.prompt: And in this one? (Airbus · closes every 3 sessions · February–April 2026)
u25l5-2.explanation: Lower and lower highs and lows: a long-only trend follower would stay out.

u25l5-3.prompt: Last chart. What trend is there? (Microsoft · closes every 3 sessions · July–September 2025)
u25l5-3.explanation: No clear direction: this is where trend strategies suffer false signals.

u25l5-4.prompt: This asset had been rising. As a trend follower, what do you think it did over the following sessions?
u25l5-4.explanation: A trend persisting more often than it reverses doesn't mean it always does: that's why you use a stop.

u25l5-5.prompt: A real chart of an index. Does it go up or down afterwards?
u25l5-5.explanation: The momentum edge is statistical, across many trades. In a single case, anything can happen.

u25l5-6.prompt: Over what time frame have trends tended to persist according to momentum studies?
u25l5-6.explanation: That's the horizon of most studies, across many markets and going back more than a century.

u25l5-10.prompt: Put the steps of a simple trend-following rule in order.
options: Enter when your rule's signal is triggered
Work out the size with 1 % risk
Put the stop below the latest higher low
Raise the stop as the trend moves on
Check there's an uptrend (higher highs and higher lows)
u25l5-10.explanation: Without the stop and the size, no trend rule survives its reversals.

u25l6-1.prompt: Swing trade: you have €10,000 and risk 1 % at most. Choose the stop and amount.
u25l6-1.explanation: Stop below the recent low and size calculated with that stop. The rest is up to the market.

u25l6-3.prompt: Swing trade on an index. Place the stop for this buy.
u25l6-3.explanation: Below the recent low: if it breaks, the pullback has turned into something else.

u25l6-4.prompt: Now place the target for this buy.
u25l6-4.explanation: Near the previous high, where selling tends to show up. Compare it with the distance to the stop.

u25l6-5.prompt: A swing trader looks for ranges and trends. What do you see here? (CaixaBank · closes every 3 sessions · May–July 2025)
u25l6-5.explanation: In a sideways market, the swing trader buys near the floor of the range and sells near the ceiling, with a stop below the floor.

u25l6-6.prompt: In a range, the target for a buy usually goes near the ceiling. Tap the highest point. (Disney · closes every 3 sessions · December 2024 – February 2025)
u25l6-6.explanation: The ceiling of the range is where selling showed up before.

u25l6-7.prompt: Match each style with its typical time frame.
u25l6-7.explanation: The shorter the time frame, the more noise and the more costs for every euro earned.
right: Minutes or hours; closes the same day

u25l7-2.prompt: In that Brazil study, what percentage earned more than the minimum wage?
u25l7-2.explanation: 1.1 %: even among the few who made money, almost none made enough to live on.

u25l7-4.prompt: Of those who day traded for more than 300 days in Brazil, ____ lost money.

u25l7-6.prompt: Why do most day traders lose? Select all that apply.
options: The costs of trading so much
u25l7-6.explanation: They compete with professionals and algorithms, and trading so much multiplies the costs; the noise on minute charts does the rest. It isn't banned and more indicators won't fix it: the maths works against you.

options: The more trades you make, the more costs weigh
Screenshots on social media show the full track record
In Taiwan, fewer than 1 % make money persistently after fees
97 % of those who day traded for more than 300 days in Brazil lost money
With €500 and a good course you can make a living from trading
u25l7-8.explanation: The facts come from studies with millions of trades; the myths, from one-off screenshots.

u25l7-10.prompt: Lumi is thinking of quitting her job to day trade because she has won 3 days in a row on the simulator. What do you say?
options: Size up now that you're on a roll
Go for it, you're a natural!
u25l7-10.explanation: Before risking your livelihood, look at the evidence and at your own stats over many trades.
feedback: A three-day streak is luck until proven otherwise: sizing up only makes the next loss bigger.
OK, I'd better keep learning, log 100 trades in the simulator and keep my job.
Three days is a ridiculously small sample… and the data says almost everyone who tries it seriously loses.
lines: I'm thinking of quitting my job to day trade 🚀
I've won 3 days in a row on the simulator.

u25l8-5.prompt: In the EU, a retail client can lose more than they've deposited when trading CFDs.
u25l8-5.explanation: Since 2018 there's been negative balance protection: you can't lose more than you deposited.

u25l8-6.prompt: Laura wants to open a CFD on an index with €1,000 and maximum leverage «to make it go further». She's never used a stop. What would you tell her, as a concept?
options: Better to go short, it's safer
Go for it, that way she makes money faster
u25l8-6.explanation: Method and risk management first; leverage, if at all, much later.
feedback: Good: leverage only amplifies what you already do. Without a method, it amplifies the mistakes.
The opposite: when you're short the potential loss is unlimited.
At 1:20, a 5 % fall in the index wipes out all her margin. That can happen in a week.

u25l8-7.prompt: Why is the loss on a short position potentially unlimited?
options: Because the broker doesn't allow stops on shorts
Because the price can rise without limit
u25l8-7.explanation: If you buy, the most you can lose is what you invested; when you're short, every euro the price rises is a loss.

u25l8-8.prompt: Match each product with the maximum CFD leverage for retail clients in the EU.
u25l8-8.explanation: The more volatile the asset, the lower the leverage allowed (ESMA, 2018).

u25l8-10.prompt: When a violent rise forces those who are short to buy back all at once, it's called a ____.
u25l8-10.explanation: Like GameStop in 2021: shorts buying back push the price up even further.

u25l9-2.prompt: Bruno works 10 hours a day and can only check his phone on breaks. He wants to start day trading. What fits him best, as a concept?
options: Day trading with leverage to make up for the lack of time
A strategy that doesn't need him watching the market
u25l9-2.explanation: The strategy has to fit into your real life.
feedback: Even worse: more risk with less attention.
Without being able to watch the screen, every trade is at the mercy of the noise. And most people lose even when doing it full-time.
Good: it fits his time and doesn't force him to make rushed decisions between meetings.

u25l9-4.prompt: Lumi wants you to tell her right now which strategy is best, «the one that makes the most». What do you reply?
options: The one that fits my time and my horizon
Whichever went up most last year: that's the one that works
u25l9-4.explanation: There's no single best strategy for everyone: there's the one you can stick to.
feedback: Exactly! A good strategy you abandon at the first fall does worse than a simple one you stick to.
Fast, yes… and the data says almost everyone loses.
That's recency bias: what did best one year rarely repeats it the next.
lines: OK, but just tell me which strategy is best 😅
The one that makes the most.

u25l9-6.prompt: How much time does each strategy need?
options: Automatic contributions to an index fund
u25l9-6.explanation: If you don't have time, choose something that works without you.

u25l9-9.prompt: Put the steps for choosing your strategy in order.
options: See how much time you can dedicate
Decide what fall you could take without selling
u25l9-9.explanation: First get to know yourself; then write the plan; finally, test it without real money.

u25l9-10.prompt: What questions do you ask yourself before choosing a strategy? Select all that apply.
options: Which one is most recommended on social media?
Which one has risen most this month?
What fall could I take without selling?
When will I need this money?
u25l9-10.explanation: When you'll need the money and what fall you could take decide which strategy you'll be able to stick to, along with the time you can give it. Whatever has risen most this month or is recommended on social media tells you nothing about you.

u25l3-12.prompt: Put a value investor's steps in order.
options: Estimating what each one is worth
Buying only if the price leaves a margin of safety
Screening for companies that are cheap according to their accounts
u25l3-12.explanation: Screen, understand, value and wait for the price: in that order.

u25l3-13.prompt: You've held a value fund for six years. Your brother-in-law, with a growth fund, has made twice as much. What do you do?
options: I switch to his: it's clear which one works
I check whether my reasons still hold
I sell everything and stay in cash
feedback: Switching to the style that has just won means buying what has already gone up, at a high price.
That's it. You choose a style knowing it will have bad years; what breaks it is abandoning it during them.
You leave the market because of a comparison, not because your plan has failed.
u25l3-13.explanation: No style wins all the time. Choose one you can stick with when it's lagging.

u25l4-13.prompt: A company pays a 2.5 % dividend and raises it every year. What does a dividend-growth investor look at?
options: Only the percentage it pays today
How far it has fallen from its high
u25l4-13.explanation: A dividend can only grow for years if profits grow with it.

u25l4-14.prompt: You collect €600 in dividends a year and they're taxed at 19 %. How much tax do you pay each year for collecting them?
u25l4-14.explanation: 600 × 0.19 = €114. In an accumulating fund, that money would stay invested until you sell.

u25l4-15.prompt: Your «dividend» portfolio holds five stocks: two banks, two utilities and a telecom. What risk do you see?
options: None: every one of them pays a good dividend
feedback: Five is few, not many.
They do pay, but they depend on the same things: a bad spell for the sector hits them all at once.
That's it: choosing by dividend has led you, without meaning to, into a sector bet.
u25l4-15.explanation: Choosing by dividend alone tends to concentrate a portfolio in a few sectors. Look at how it's spread too.

u25l4-16.prompt: A fund that pays out more dividends gives, for that very reason, a higher total return.
u25l4-16.explanation: Total return is price plus dividends. What's paid out comes out of the fund's value.
